newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission leaves out job graphs in report.
newsitem.headline: Commission leaves out job graphs in report.

text.p: The European Commission, furious over "cowboy" reports of an internal row, released graphs on Friday showing an alleged link between unemployment and rigid labour laws but said they would be left out of a formal report.

The Commission said it was releasing the disputed graphs to show that it was not trying to conceal them even though it had been decided not to include them in an upcoming report on EU industry competitiveness.
The issue reportedly sparked a row between the Commission's offices for industry -- where the report was written -- and for social affairs, which sought to suppress the graphs.
Explaining why the graphs would not be included, Commission spokesman Nikolaus van der Pas said the correlation shown between unemployment and strict social legislation was weak.
"That is the very reason why we felt this was not sufficient evidence or support for this to include it in the final document," van der Pas told reporters.

He said there had been ridiculous claims in some newspapers" that we've been trying to to remove or overrule a Commission document" and that the reports had angered Commission President Jacques Santer.
"Really, the discussion has been absurd," he added, describing the reports as "cowboy stories."
However, the controversy highlights a heated debate in the EU on whether strict labour market legislation is a key factor behind the high unemployment rate of 11 percent.
Even without the graphs, van der Pas said the basic message of the report was that there were "difficulties for creating employment when it comes to rigidity of legislation."
One of the graphs in the soon-to-be-published report concerns the relationship between employment and regulations in the EU while the other links jobs with costs for dismissing workers.
"While there is some indication that labour market regulation affects employment creation, the evidence is not conclusive," the text accompanying the graphs said.
It also said that "it appears that when termination costs are high firms tend to adopt a cautious recruitment policy."
"In times of recession, firing costs prevent downsizing. Similarly, in times of economic recovery, firms will be reluctant to take on employees," the text added.

John Richardson, secretary general of the European Round Table of Industrialists, said the most important was to get the report published. "This kind of disagreement doesn't do the Commission any real credit," he told Reuters.
He said there was no doubt of the relationship between regulations and employment. "If you have a regime with high regulation that will have a negative effect on employment."
An official at the European employers' group UNICE sharply criticised the Commission's handling of the issue.

UNICE this month warned that the EU's competitiveness continued to decline and it was time to study whether the functioning of the labour market itself was a major cause behind Europe's high unemployment rate.
